text:
Suppose a program is running on a non-pipelined single processor computer system. The computer is connected to an external device that can interrupt the processor asynchronously. The processor needs to execute the interrupt service routine (ISR) to serve this interrupt. The following steps (not necessarily in order) are taken by the processor when the interrupt arrives:

(i) The processor saves the content of the program counter.
(ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR.
(iii) The processor finishes the present instruction.

Which ONE of the following is the CORRECT sequence of steps?
solution:
On an asynchronous interrupt, the processor must first reach a clean state before it can safely switch control:

1. (iii) The processor finishes the present instruction — interrupts are only serviced at instruction boundaries, never mid-instruction.
2. (i) The processor saves the content of the program counter — so execution can later resume exactly where it left off.
3. (ii) The program counter is loaded with the start address of the ISR — only now does control actually transfer to the ISR.

Answer: (iii), (i), (ii)

text: Which ONE of the following statements is FALSE regarding the symbol table?
solution:
Checking each statement about the symbol table:

- It tracks variable scope — true, this is one of its core jobs.
- It can be implemented using a BST — true, BSTs (or hash tables) are standard implementations.
- It is created during lexical analysis — true, entries are typically first added as identifiers are tokenized.
- "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" — FALSE. The symbol table is essential well beyond parsing: semantic analysis (type checking), intermediate code generation, and code optimization (e.g. register allocation) all continue to rely on it.

Answer: "Symbol table is not required after the parsing phase" is FALSE.

text: Which ONE of the following techniques used in compiler code optimization uses live variable analysis?
solution:
Live variable analysis determines, at each point in the program, which variables' current values might still be used later (i.e. are "live"). This information is exactly what's needed to decide which variables are worth keeping in fast registers versus which can be safely evicted — that's the core of register allocation/assignment.

Run-time function call management, strength reduction, and constant folding are all real optimizations, but none of them fundamentally depend on liveness information the way register allocation does.

Answer: Register assignment to variables

text: Consider a demand paging memory management system with 32-bit logical address, 20-bit physical address, and page size of 2048 bytes. Assuming that the memory is byte addressable, what is the maximum number of entries in the page table?
solution:
Page size [latex]=2048=2^{11}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset field needs [latex]11[/latex] bits.

With a [latex]32[/latex]-bit logical address, the remaining bits form the page number: [latex]32-11=21[/latex] bits.

The page table needs one entry per possible page number, so the maximum number of entries [latex]=2^{21}[/latex].

Answer: [latex]2^{21}[/latex]

text:
[latex]g(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]B[/latex], [latex]f(. )[/latex] is a function from [latex]B[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex], and their composition defined as [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] is a mapping from [latex]A[/latex] to [latex]C[/latex].
If [latex]f(. )[/latex] and [latex]f(g(. ))[/latex] are onto (surjective) functions, which ONE of the following is TRUE about the function [latex]g(. )[/latex]?
solution:
We're told [latex]f[/latex] is onto (B→C) and the composite [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is onto (A→C), and asked what this forces about [latex]g[/latex] (A→B).

Intuitively: since [latex]f[/latex] alone is already onto [latex]C[/latex], every element of [latex]C[/latex] has some preimage in [latex]B[/latex] regardless of [latex]g[/latex]. The fact that [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is also onto just says [latex]g[/latex]'s image happens to hit enough of [latex]B[/latex] to cover all of [latex]f[/latex]'s "useful" preimages — but [latex]g[/latex] itself doesn't need to be onto all of [latex]B[/latex] (there could be elements of [latex]B[/latex] entirely outside [latex]g[/latex]'s range, as long as [latex]f[/latex] still reaches every element of [latex]C[/latex] through the range [latex]g[/latex] does cover), nor does [latex]g[/latex] need to be one-to-one (multiple elements of [latex]A[/latex] could map to the same element of [latex]B[/latex]).

A simple counterexample confirms it: let [latex]B=\{1,2\}[/latex], [latex]C=\{1\}[/latex], [latex]f[/latex] onto, and [latex]g[/latex] mapping every element of [latex]A[/latex] to just [latex]1\in B[/latex] — [latex]g[/latex] is neither onto nor one-to-one, yet [latex]f\circ g[/latex] is trivially onto.

Answer: g(.) is not required to be a one-to-one or onto function.

text: Let [latex]G[/latex] be any undirected graph with positive edge weights, and [latex]T[/latex] be a minimum spanning tree of [latex]G[/latex]. For any two vertices, [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex], let [latex]d_1(u, v)[/latex] and [latex]d_2(u, v)[/latex] be the shortest distances between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex] and [latex]T[/latex], respectively. Which ONE of the options is CORRECT for all possible [latex]G[/latex], [latex]T[/latex], [latex]u[/latex], and [latex]v[/latex]?
solution:
[latex]T[/latex] is a subgraph of [latex]G[/latex] using only a subset of [latex]G[/latex]'s edges, so any path that exists inside [latex]T[/latex] between [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] is also a valid path in [latex]G[/latex] (with the exact same total weight). This means the shortest path in [latex]G[/latex] can never be longer than the shortest path in [latex]T[/latex] — [latex]G[/latex] has strictly more routing options available (all of [latex]T[/latex]'s edges, plus possibly more), so it can only match or beat [latex]T[/latex]'s best distance.

So [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex] always holds (equality is common but not guaranteed — a shortcut through a non-tree edge in [latex]G[/latex] can make [latex]d_1[/latex] strictly smaller).

Answer: [latex]d_1(u,v)\le d_2(u,v)[/latex]

text:
Consider the following context-free grammar [latex]G[/latex], where [latex]S[/latex], [latex]A[/latex], and [latex]B[/latex] are the variables (non-terminals), [latex]a[/latex] and [latex]b[/latex] are the terminal symbols, [latex]S[/latex] is the start variable, and the rules of [latex]G[/latex] are described as:

[latex]S \to aaB \mid Abb[/latex]
[latex]A \to a \mid aA[/latex]
[latex]B \to b \mid bB[/latex]

Which ONE of the languages [latex]L(G)[/latex] is accepted by [latex]G[/latex]?
solution:
[latex]A\to a\mid aA[/latex] generates exactly the strings [latex]a^n[/latex] for [latex]n\ge1[/latex] (one or more [latex]a[/latex]'s), and similarly [latex]B\to b\mid bB[/latex] generates [latex]b^n[/latex] for [latex]n\ge1[/latex].

So:
- [latex]S\to aaB[/latex] generates [latex]aa[/latex] followed by [latex]b^n[/latex] ([latex]n\ge1[/latex]), i.e. the set [latex]\{a^2b^n\mid n\ge1\}[/latex].

[latex]L(G)[/latex] is the union of these two alternatives.

Answer: [latex]L(G)=\{a^2b^n\mid n\ge1\}\cup\{a^nb^2\mid n\ge1\}[/latex]

Consider the following recurrence relation:

[latex]T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n \quad \text{for} \quad n > 0, \quad T(0) = 1[/latex]

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
solution:
[latex]T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]. Substitute [latex]T(n)=2^nS(n)[/latex]:
[latex]2^nS(n)=2\cdot2^{n-1}S(n-1)+n2^n=2^nS(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]

So [latex]T(n)=2^n\cdot\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex]

text: Consider the following [latex]B^+[/latex] tree with 5 nodes, in which a node can store at most 3 key values. The value 23 is now inserted in the [latex]B^+[/latex] tree. Which of the following options(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
Inserting a new key into a [latex]B^+[/latex] tree always follows the same pattern: search down to the correct leaf, insert the key there in sorted order, and if that leaf now holds more than the maximum allowed keys (here, more than [latex]3[/latex]), it must split into two leaves, pushing/copying up a separator key into the parent.

Since the target leaf here is already at its maximum capacity of [latex]3[/latex] keys before inserting [latex]23[/latex], it overflows and must split; this new separator key then gets inserted into the parent node, which can itself overflow and split further, potentially propagating all the way up to a new root. Whenever a split reaches (or creates a new) root, the height of the tree increases by one level. Splitting always increases the total node count (a leaf becomes two, or an internal node splits into two) — it never leaves the count unchanged, and "no node splits" is only possible if the target leaf had spare capacity, which it did not here.

Answer: At least one node will split and redistribute; and the height of the tree will increase.

text: Consider the 3-way handshaking protocol for TCP connection establishment. Let the three packets exchanged during the connection establishment be denoted as P1, P2, and P3, in order. Which of the following option(s) is/are TRUE with respect to TCP header flags that are set in the packets?
solution:
TCP's 3-way handshake, packet by packet:

- P1 (client → server): the client initiates with SYN=1 (and ACK=0, since there's nothing to acknowledge yet).
- P2 (server → client): the server both acknowledges the client's SYN and sends its own SYN, so SYN=1, ACK=1 simultaneously (this combined SYN-ACK packet is the hallmark of TCP's handshake).
- P3 (client → server): the client only needs to acknowledge the server's SYN, so SYN=0, ACK=1 (not SYN=1,ACK=1 as one distractor suggests).

So the correct flags are P1: SYN=1, and P2: SYN=1 & ACK=1.

Answer: P2 (SYN=1, ACK=1), and P1 (SYN=1)

text:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

[latex]x + k y = 1[/latex]
[latex]k x + y = -1[/latex]
solution:
[latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex].

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

There exist an infinite number of values of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has no solution.

text: Let [latex]X[/latex] be a 3-variable Boolean function that produces output as '1' when at least two of the input variables are '1'. Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT, where [latex]a, b, c, d, e[/latex] are Boolean variables?
solution:
[latex]X[/latex] is the 3-input majority function: [latex]X(p,q,r)=1[/latex] iff at least [latex]2[/latex] of [latex]p,q,r[/latex] are [latex]1[/latex]. A useful fact: whenever two of the three inputs to [latex]X[/latex] are the same variable [latex]v[/latex], the output is forced to equal [latex]v[/latex] regardless of the third input (e.g. [latex]X(v,v,\text{anything})=v[/latex]).

Checking [latex]X(a,b,X(a,b,c))=X(a,b,c)[/latex]: let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex], then [latex]m=a[/latex] too, and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,a,a)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex], then (since one of [latex]a,b[/latex] is [latex]0[/latex] and the other [latex]1[/latex]) [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,b,m)=X(a,b,c)=m[/latex]. Either way it checks out. True.

Checking [latex]X(a,b,c)=X(a,X(a,b,c),X(a,c,c))[/latex]: note [latex]X(a,c,c)=c[/latex] (two matching inputs). Let [latex]m=X(a,b,c)[/latex]. If [latex]a=b[/latex]: [latex]m=a[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,a,c)=a=m[/latex]. If [latex]a\ne b[/latex]: [latex]m=c[/latex], and [latex]X(a,m,c)=X(a,c,c)=c=m[/latex]. Checks out both ways. True.

The other two options can be shown false with a direct counterexample assignment of [latex]a,b,c,d[/latex] (the two sides disagree for some input combination) — they do not hold as general identities.

Answer: X(a,b,X(a,b,c)) = X(a,b,c); and X(a,b,c) = X(a, X(a,b,c), X(a,c,c))

text: The number [latex]-6[/latex] can be represented as 1010 in 4-bit 2's complement representation. Which of the following is/are CORRECT 2's complement representation(s) of [latex]-6[/latex]?
solution:
Correctly extending a two's-complement number to more bits requires sign-extension: replicate the sign bit (here, the leading [latex]1[/latex], since [latex]-6[/latex] is negative) into all the new higher-order bit positions — you cannot just prepend arbitrary/zero bits.

[latex]-6[/latex] in 4-bit: [latex]1010[/latex].
Correct 8-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1010[/latex] (four [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,1010[/latex] incorrectly prepends [latex]1000[/latex] instead of replicating the sign bit — wrong.
Correct 16-bit sign-extension: [latex]1111\,1111\,1111\,1010[/latex] (twelve [latex]1[/latex]'s prepended). The alternative [latex]1000\,0000\,0000\,1010[/latex] is similarly wrong.

Answer: 1111 1010 (8-bit) and 1111 1111 1111 1010 (16-bit)

text: Which of the following statement(s) is/are TRUE for any binary search tree (BST) having [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers?
solution:
Checking each BST claim for [latex]n[/latex] distinct integers:

- Maximum path length from root to any node is [latex]n-1[/latex]: true — in the worst case (a completely skewed/degenerate BST, essentially a linked list), all [latex]n[/latex] nodes form a single chain, giving a root-to-deepest-node path of [latex]n-1[/latex] edges, which is also the largest this can ever be since there are only [latex]n[/latex] nodes total.
- Inorder traversal always produces sorted order: true — this is the defining property of a BST (left subtree [latex]<[/latex] node [latex]<[/latex] right subtree, recursively), and it holds regardless of the tree's shape.
- Finding an element takes [latex]O(\log_2n)[/latex] time in the worst case: false — that bound only holds for a balanced BST. A skewed/degenerate BST (as noted above) can force search time all the way up to [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Every BST is also a Min-Heap: false — a min-heap requires every parent to be smaller than both children, but a BST only orders left [latex]<[/latex] parent [latex]<[/latex] right; nothing stops a BST's left child from being smaller than its grandparent in ways that violate heap order.

Answer: Max path length is n-1; and inorder traversal always gives sorted order.

text: A regular language [latex]L[/latex] is accepted by a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with [latex]n[/latex] states. Which of the following statement(s) is/are FALSE?
solution:
For a regular language [latex]L[/latex] accepted by some [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA, recall two standard facts: (1) subset construction always produces an equivalent DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states, and (2) NFA/DFA state counts for a given language are not unique — smaller equivalent automata can certainly exist.

- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting NFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": could well be true (this [latex]n[/latex]-state NFA might not be minimal), so calling it FALSE is incorrect — it's a true possibility, not a false statement.
- "[latex]L[/latex] may have an accepting DFA with [latex]< n[/latex] states": also entirely possible depending on the language, so this is also true (not false).
- "There exists a DFA with [latex]\le 2^n[/latex] states accepting [latex]L[/latex]": guaranteed true by subset construction — so this is also true, not false.
- "Every DFA that accepts L has [latex]> 2^n[/latex] states": this directly contradicts the subset-construction guarantee (a DFA with at most [latex]2^n[/latex] states always exists) — so this statement is definitely FALSE.

Answer: "Every DFA that accepts L has more than [latex]2^n[/latex] states" is the FALSE statement.

text:
Which of the following predicate logic formulae/formula is/are CORRECT representation(s) of the statement: "Everyone has exactly one mother"?

The meanings of the predicates used are:
[latex]mother(y,x): y[/latex] is the mother of [latex] x [/latex]
[latex]noteq(x,y): x[/latex] and [latex] y [/latex] are not equal
solution:
We want: for every person [latex]x[/latex], there is exactly one [latex]y[/latex] who is [latex]x[/latex]'s mother — meaning both existence (someone is the mother) and uniqueness (nobody else also qualifies as a distinct mother).

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))][/latex]: says "[latex]y[/latex] is a mother of [latex]x[/latex], and every [latex]z[/latex] different from [latex]y[/latex] is not a mother of [latex]x[/latex]" — this correctly captures existence plus uniqueness. Correct.

[latex]\forall x\exists y[mother(y,x)\wedge\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))][/latex]: by De Morgan's law, [latex]\neg\exists z(noteq(z,y)\wedge mother(z,x))[/latex] is logically identical to [latex]\forall z(noteq(z,y)\to\neg mother(z,x))[/latex] — so this is just a different (but equivalent) way of writing the same correct statement above. Correct.

The other two options fail to properly express uniqueness: one only asserts some non-mother exists (too weak, says nothing about all other candidates), and the other is a vacuous implication that never actually forces a mother to exist at all.

Answer: Both the ∀x∃y[...∀z(noteq→¬mother)] form and its De Morgan-equivalent ∀x∃y[...¬∃z(noteq∧mother)] form are correct.

text:
[latex] A = \{ 0,1,2,3,\dots \} [/latex] is the set of non-negative integers. Let [latex] {F} [/latex] be the set of functions from [latex] A [/latex] to itself. For any two functions, [latex] f_1, f_2 \in {F} [/latex], we define

[latex] (f_1 \odot f_2)(n) = f_1(n) + f_2(n)[/latex]

for every number [latex] n [/latex] in [latex] A [/latex]. Which of the following is/are CORRECT about the mathematical structure [latex] ({F}, \odot ) [/latex]?
solution:
[latex](f_1\odot f_2)(n)=f_1(n)+f_2(n)[/latex] — pointwise addition of functions into the non-negative integers.

- Closure: the sum of two non-negative-integer values is still a non-negative integer, so [latex]F[/latex] is closed under [latex]\odot[/latex].
- Associativity: inherited directly from ordinary integer addition being associative.
- Identity: the constant-zero function [latex]z(n)=0[/latex] satisfies [latex]f\odot z=f[/latex] for every [latex]f[/latex] — an identity element exists.
- Commutativity: [latex]f_1(n)+f_2(n)=f_2(n)+f_1(n)[/latex] pointwise, so [latex]\odot[/latex] is commutative.
- Inverses: for a general [latex]f[/latex] (e.g. [latex]f(n)=n[/latex]), we'd need some [latex]g[/latex] with [latex]f(n)+g(n)=0[/latex], forcing [latex]g(n)=-f(n)[/latex] — but negative values aren't allowed in the codomain [latex]A[/latex]. So inverses generally don't exist.

Since it's closed, associative, has an identity, and is commutative, but lacks inverses, [latex](F,\odot)[/latex] is exactly an Abelian monoid (not a group).

Answer: (F, ⊙) is an Abelian monoid.
